editorNote: Late May 1983 finds Apple II players digging through new mazes while inexpensive home computers crowd the review bench and music software pushes the machine toward the studio.
morningLine: Lode Runner climbs the Apple II conversation as budget micros and music systems fill the May magazines.

lead.headline: Lode Runner gives Apple II players 150 rooms to conquer
lead.dek: Softalk's 1983 software record puts Doug Smith's run-climb-dig game among the year's defining Apple II releases, complete with a construction set for making new levels.
lead.body: Broderbund's Lode Runner turns a simple chase into a toolbox: collect the gold, outwit the guards, and then design another screen. Its mix of arcade pace and player-made levels captures the spring's most exciting computer-game idea—software that lets the owner become part designer.
lead.confidence: 1983 Softalk software record and contemporary Apple II coverage; treated as May 1983 shelf context rather than an exact release-day claim.

computerItems.title: Softalk tunes the Apple II for the studio
computerItems.summary: The May issue profiles Herbie Hancock and the Syntauri professional music system, showing the Apple II reaching beyond games and ledgers into composition and performance.

computerItems.title: Creative Computing tests another wave of budget micros
computerItems.summary: May reviews put the Panasonic JR-200, Video Technology VZ200, and TI 99/4A side by side in an increasingly crowded low-cost home-computer field.

computerItems.title: Atari BASIC pilots race through Starshot
computerItems.summary: COMPUTE!'s May Starshot program sends Atari owners down a trench in a type-in game that also demonstrates how machine-language help can lift BASIC action.

computerItems.title: Modem games enter the hobbyist playbook
computerItems.summary: Computer Gaming World's May-June cover makes modem gaming part of the dedicated computer-gamer's agenda alongside adventures, baseball leagues, and strategy titles.
